0.title: He Must Increase, I Must Decrease
0.essay:
Pride is the sin we see most easily in others and least easily in ourselves. It is often called the root of all other sins, because at heart it is the desire to be our own god. Humility, by contrast, is one of the most attractive qualities a person can have — and one of the hardest to pursue, because the moment we think we have it, we have lost it.

Grace flows downhill

Scripture speaks of pride and humility again and again. “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). That one sentence explains why humility matters so much. Grace flows downhill, to the low places. The proud shut themselves off from the very grace they need.

The goal

John the Baptist summed it up when his disciples worried that everyone was going after Jesus: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). That is the goal of this study — not self-hatred, but a life in which Christ is more and more, and we are content to be less.

The chapters

Pride: The Root Sin; The Humility of Christ; God Opposes the Proud; What Humility Looks Like; and Growing in Humility.

1.title: Pride: The Root Sin
1.essay:
The serpent’s temptation in Eden appealed to pride: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). Adam and Eve were not content to be creatures. They wanted to decide for themselves what was good. Every sin since has carried the same seed: putting ourselves in God’s place.

Pride in disguise

That was the hook. And pride rarely presents itself as rebellion. It presents itself as wisdom, freedom or self-fulfilment. But at its root it is the desire to be our own authority, refusing the place God has given us.

Pride is an inflated view of ourselves and a deflated view of God. It shows itself in boasting, self-righteousness, a critical spirit, an unteachable heart, a need for praise, resentment when overlooked, refusal to admit wrong and contempt for others. It can even hide behind false humility, in people who talk constantly about their failures so that others will reassure them.

The most dangerous pride is religious: pride in our knowledge, our gifts, our morality or our doctrinal correctness. Jesus’ harshest words were for the proud religious leaders of his day.

Pride deceives

“The pride of your heart has deceived you” (Obadiah 3). Edom lived in rocky strongholds and felt untouchable. God answered, “Though you soar aloft like the eagle, though your nest is set among the stars, from there I will bring you down” (Obadiah 4). No height is high enough to escape God. Pride makes us feel secure precisely when we are most in danger, and blinds us to our weakness.

Pride goes before a fall

“Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall. It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud” (Proverbs 16:18–19). Humility with poverty is better than pride with wealth. God’s values turn the world’s upside down.

King Nebuchadnezzar walked on his palace roof and said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30). The words were barely out of his mouth when he was humbled, driven from people to live like an animal, until he learned “that the Most High rules the kingdom of men” (Daniel 4:32). When his reason returned, he praised the King of heaven, confessing that “those who walk in pride he is able to humble” (Daniel 4:37). The proudest king on earth learned humility the hard way.

King Uzziah was greatly blessed and became powerful. “But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction” (2 Chronicles 26:16). He entered the temple to burn incense, a task reserved for priests, and was struck with leprosy. Success is often more dangerous to the soul than failure.

God hates pride

Among the things the Lord hates, the first listed is “haughty eyes” (Proverbs 6:17). “Pride and arrogance and the way of evil and perverted speech I hate” (Proverbs 8:13). Pride is not a small fault. It is a direct challenge to God’s glory.

Not low self-esteem

Our culture often treats low self-esteem as the main human problem. Scripture says our deeper problem is that we think too much of ourselves and too little of God. Humility is not thinking badly of ourselves but thinking rightly — and thinking of ourselves less.

Not all pride is sinful. Paul can say, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31), and tell the Corinthians, “I have great pride in you” (2 Corinthians 7:4). A craftsman may rightly be satisfied with good work. Sinful pride takes credit for what God has given and lifts us above others.

The test

A capable church leader is praised often for his preaching. Slowly he begins to resent anyone who questions him and to speak dismissively of other churches. A friend lovingly points this out. At first he is defensive. Then he sees it, confesses his pride and asks for prayer. His ministry becomes gentler and more fruitful.

How do you react when you are corrected, overlooked or criticised? Your reaction reveals how much pride is in you.

For reflection

In what forms does pride most often show itself in your life? Why is it so hard to see in ourselves? Read Daniel 4: what did Nebuchadnezzar learn, and how? Is there an area of success in your life that could become a source of pride?

2.title: The Humility of Christ
2.essay:
The greatest example of humility is not a saint or a monk but the Son of God himself.

He emptied himself

“Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:5–8). The one who had every right to glory chose the lowest place. Humility is not weakness; it is strength choosing to serve.

Paul’s command around this hymn is practical: “in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others” (Philippians 2:3–4). And the outcome follows: “Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). Humility now, glory later. The path to glory ran through humility, and that is the pattern for his followers too.

Notice too the words “which is yours in Christ Jesus”. We do not produce humility by imitation alone. We grow in it as Christ lives in us by his Spirit.

He washed feet

On the night before his death, “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist” (John 13:3–4), and washed his disciples’ feet, the task of the lowest servant. John notes what Jesus knew before he took the towel. Supreme security led to supreme service. He knew who he was, so he did not need to prove it. Peter protested, but Jesus insisted, and then said, “For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you” (John 13:15). Christian leadership is foot-washing leadership.

Believers secure in God’s love are free to serve in the same way, without needing recognition. A successful businesswoman volunteers at her church’s community meal and is assigned to wash dishes in the back kitchen, where no one sees her. At first she is irritated. Then she remembers John 13 and finds joy in the hidden work. It becomes the highlight of her week.

Gentle and lowly

Jesus described himself in these terms: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:29–30). Why should the weary come to him? Because he is not a harsh master. The Lord of the universe is approachable. He welcomed children, ate with sinners and touched lepers. The humility of Christ is not only our example; it is our comfort. He welcomes the weak.

He came to serve

When James and John asked for the best seats in the kingdom, the other disciples were indignant, probably because they wanted the same seats. Jesus called them together and contrasted the rulers of the nations, who lord it over others, with his followers: “But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:43–45). He was on his way to the cross even as they argued about thrones. Greatness in God’s kingdom is measured by service.

Humility is Godlike

We might think humility belongs only to creatures. But Christ’s humility reveals something about God himself. The Son delights to serve the Father’s purpose, and the high and holy God stoops to dwell “with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit” (Isaiah 57:15). Humility is part of the beauty of God’s own character.

Are you willing to do tasks that no one will see or thank you for?

For reflection

What does Philippians 2:5–8 teach about the nature of true humility? Why did Jesus’ security free him to wash his disciples’ feet? How does his description of himself as “gentle and lowly” change how you come to him? What hidden act of service could you do this week?

3.title: God Opposes the Proud
3.essay:
“But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble’” (James 4:6). Quoted by both James and Peter from Proverbs 3:34, it is one of the most sobering statements in Scripture.

God sets himself against the proud

God actively resists the proud. He sets himself against them. But to the humble he gives grace, and more grace. James follows the proverb with a string of commands: submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, cleanse your hands, purify your hearts, grieve over sin. And the promise frames it all: “Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10).

Two men praying

Jesus told a parable “to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt” (Luke 18:9). A Pharisee stood and thanked God that he was not like other men, and listed his religious achievements. His prayer was all about himself: what he was not, what he did. A tax collector stood far off, would not even lift his eyes, beat his breast and prayed, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” His prayer was all about God’s mercy; he compared himself with no one. Jesus’ verdict shocked his hearers: “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:13–14). Humility, not performance, receives God’s grace.

A man has been coming to church for years, proud of his good life and generous giving. One Sunday, hearing Luke 18 preached, he realises he has been praying like the Pharisee. For the first time he prays the tax collector’s prayer and means it. He later says that was the day he became a Christian.

The poor in spirit

Pride is the great barrier to salvation. The proud do not think they need a Saviour; only those who see their sin and helplessness turn to Christ. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3). The kingdom belongs to spiritual beggars.

The Reformed doctrines of grace are deeply humbling for exactly this reason. If salvation is entirely God’s work, “not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:9), then there is nothing left to be proud of. “What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). Grace kills pride at the root.

The one God looks to

God says heaven is his throne and earth his footstool; no temple could contain him. Yet he says, “But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word” (Isaiah 66:2). Greatness does not impress God; humility does. He draws near to the humble. Proud prayers bounce off the ceiling; humble cries reach his heart.

Humble yourselves

Peter writes, “Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for ‘God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:5–7). The picture of clothing suggests a servant tying on an apron. And notice the link with anxiety. Anxiety often comes from trying to control what only God controls. Humility accepts our limits and trusts his care. It is not only an attitude to others; it is trust in God. Humility is something we choose, and God promises to lift up those who do.

That promise may be fulfilled in this life, and it will certainly be fulfilled in the next. Mary sang that God “has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate” (Luke 1:52).

Naaman in the river

Naaman, commander of the Syrian army, came to Elisha to be healed of leprosy. When told to wash seven times in the Jordan, he was furious; he had expected something grander. His servants persuaded him to obey. When he humbled himself and went down into the river, “his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean” (2 Kings 5:14).

When you pray, do you come more like the Pharisee or the tax collector?

For reflection

What does it mean that God “opposes” the proud? Read Luke 18:9–14: which character are you more like? How do the doctrines of grace humble us? Which anxieties do you need to cast on God as an act of humility?

4.title: What Humility Looks Like
4.essay:
Humility is not a feeling but a way of life. Scripture shows what it looks like in practice.

Thinking rightly about ourselves

“For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned” (Romans 12:3). Humility does not deny our gifts but sees them accurately, as gifts from God to be used for others. Paul goes straight on to say that we are all members of one body, each with different gifts. No member is self-sufficient. Humility recognises both our gifts and our need of others.

The Corinthians were puffed up, taking sides with different leaders. Paul asked three questions: “For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). Every gift, talent and advantage we have was given. There is nothing left to boast about.

Putting others first

“Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves” (Philippians 2:3). Humility notices others’ needs and puts them ahead of our own convenience.

Being teachable

“Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid” (Proverbs 12:1). A humble person can receive correction and learn from anyone, including those who are younger, less educated or less experienced.

Admitting wrong

Humble people say “I was wrong” and “Please forgive me” without excuses. Proud people defend, blame and justify.

Not seeking praise

“Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring. Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (Proverbs 27:1–2). Humility is honest about our limits and leaves our reputation in God’s hands. Jesus warned, “Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them” (Matthew 6:1). Humble people are content to be overlooked.

At home with the lowly

“Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight” (Romans 12:16). Humility does not seek out only the important or impressive. It is at home with anyone.

Rejoicing in others’ success

Humble people can celebrate when others are honoured, even rivals. John the Baptist was the most famous prophet of his day, with crowds coming from all over Judea. When Jesus appeared, John pointed his own disciples to him: “Behold, the Lamb of God!” (John 1:36), and two of them left John and followed Jesus. When his disciples later complained that everyone was going to Jesus, John said he was only the friend of the bridegroom: “Therefore this joy of mine is now complete. He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:29–30). Those words are a motto for every Christian. Our joy is in seeing Christ honoured, not ourselves.

A senior pastor notices that his younger assistant’s preaching is better received than his own. He feels a stab of jealousy. Then he confesses it to God and decides to give the young man more opportunities to preach. He tells the church, “God has given us a gift in this brother.” The young man never forgets it.

Humble and bold

Humility is not timidity. Paul was humble and bold. “Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth” (Numbers 12:3), yet he confronted Pharaoh. Humility rests its confidence on God, not on self.

Leaders are especially tempted to pride. Scripture warns that an elder “must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit” (1 Timothy 3:6). Humble leaders listen, share credit, admit mistakes and serve.

And humility shapes how we disagree. Humble Christians can hold firm convictions while recognising that they may be wrong on secondary matters, listening carefully to others and speaking gently.

When someone else is praised for something you are good at, what do you feel?

For reflection

Which mark of humility is weakest in your life? How did you respond the last time you were corrected? Read 1 Corinthians 4:7: what gifts are you tempted to boast about as if you earned them? Whose success could you celebrate this week, even if it is hard?

5.title: Growing in Humility
5.essay:
No one becomes humble by trying to feel humble. Humility grows as we see God and ourselves rightly, and Scripture shows several ways.

Look at God

When Isaiah saw the Lord, he cried, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5). When Job heard God speak from the whirlwind, he said, “therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:6). Nothing humbles us like a true sight of God’s greatness and holiness.

“When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?” (Psalm 8:3–4). Yet God has crowned humanity with glory and honour and given them dominion over his works. Humility and dignity belong together: we are small, but loved. And the psalm begins and ends not with our name but with his: “O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!” (Psalm 8:9).

When did you last spend time simply looking at God’s greatness, in creation or in Scripture, until you felt small?

Look at the cross

The cross shows how serious our sin is: it took the death of God’s Son to forgive it. And it shows how great God’s love is. No one can stand at the cross and feel proud.

Accept God’s humbling

God often humbles his children through weakness, failure, illness or disappointment. Paul was given “a thorn … in the flesh” after extraordinary revelations, “to keep me from becoming conceited” (2 Corinthians 12:7). He pleaded three times for it to be removed, and God answered, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). So Paul learned to boast in his weaknesses: “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10). Hard providences, received rightly, are schools of humility.

A man who prided himself on his independence suffers a stroke and must depend on others for everything. At first he is bitter. Slowly, as his church family cares for him, he learns to receive help with gratitude. He tells his pastor, “I think God had to take away my strength to teach me humility. I’m grateful, though I wouldn’t have chosen it.”

Choose the lower place

Jesus watched guests scramble for the best seats at a dinner, and told them to take the lowest place instead, so that the host might say, “Friend, move up higher” (Luke 14:10). Better to be invited up than sent down. Then the principle: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). God is the host, and he decides who sits where. Humility can be practised: choosing to serve, to listen, to give way, to take the less noticed role.

Quieten your soul

“O LORD, my heart is not lifted up; my eyes are not raised too high; I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me. But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child is my soul within me. O Israel, hope in the LORD” (Psalm 131:1–3). It is a picture of humble contentment: a child no longer demanding, simply resting with its mother. Humility brings rest. The proud are restless, always comparing, always striving to prove themselves. The humble rest in God, and are free to enjoy God, others and life without the burden of self-promotion. Humility and hope go together.

Pray for it

Humility is a grace from God. Ask him for it honestly, knowing that he may answer through humbling circumstances.

Forgetting ourselves

The goal is not endless self-examination for signs of pride, which can itself become self-absorbed. The goal is to be so taken up with Christ and with others that we think about ourselves less.

And it is never finished. Even mature Christians struggle with pride, and the fight goes on until glory. But Paul shows the direction of growth. In letters written over several years he called himself “the least of the apostles” (1 Corinthians 15:9), then “the very least of all the saints” (Ephesians 3:8), and finally the “foremost” of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). Growing in Christ did not make him think more of himself, but less. God is patient, and he finishes what he starts.

For reflection

How has seeing God’s greatness humbled you? Has God used weakness or failure to humble you, and what did you learn? What is one way you could “take the lower place” this week? Read Psalm 131 slowly and pray it as your own.
